newsitem.title: UK: Yen's fate casts long shadow over G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Yen's fate casts long shadow over G7 summit.

text.p: It's bad, it's bothersome for financial markets and it's back.
Not for the first time, trade friction between Japan and the United States threatens to dominate a Group of Seven (G7) summit and to shake up the dollar/yen exchange rate.
Unless G7 leaders, meeting this weekend in Denver, show concern about a rising Japanese trade surplus, yen bulls will feel free to charge again, economists said on Friday.
This could have a ripple-effect for bond buyers, who in the past used Japan's paltry interest rates to finance their bond purchases, they added.

"The growing trade surplus that the Japanese have is obviously of concern, purely for historical reasons," said Henry Wilkes, treasurer at Bank Julius Baer in London. "The last time this happened the U.S. used the currency as a weapon."

That was in the months leading to April 1995, when the dollar fell to 79.70 yen, a post-World War Two low. U.S. officials, upset by persistently high Japanese surpluses and slow progress at dismantling trade barriers, did little to stop the dollar's freefall.
Mark Cliffe, chief international economist at HSBC Markets in London, said that although the Japanese were trying to play down the trade issue, it would almost certainly be raised at the G7 summit.
"The question that really arises is can the Japanese offer something at Denver that will placate the Americans? Otherwise this will be an ongoing problem for the dollar," Cliffe said.
Not so long ago, there were concerns about the yen's weakness. But that has all changed now.
The dollar zoomed higher to a 127.46 peak in early May before shedding nearly 17 yen in a matter of weeks. At 1028 GMT it was at 114.52/62 yen.
A prime reason, analysts said, has been a turnaround in perceptions. They now think Japan's economy is picking up at a time when U.S. growth has shown signs of slowing.
Against this background, trade numbers have come into sharp focus. Japan's global surplus in May rose more than 200 percent from a year earlier. Its surplus with the U.S. increased 90 percent.

"My fear is that G7 provides no guidance," said Mark Fox, chief European strategist, fixed income, at Lehman Brothers in London. "If the G7 simply ignores the trade issue that could well be interpreted by the market as a sign that they are free to take the yen higher."
That could have big ramifications for bonds.

When everything seemed to be going the dollar's way, many people conducted so-called carry trades. They borrowed cheaply in yen, bought dollars or other currencies, and invested in higher-yielding bond markets.
But the yen's resurgence cost them dearly.

Fox, however, said that given the yen's move since May, carry trades might come into vogue again. If the G7 did come out with a strong message on trade, and people grew comfortable with the idea the dollar would not fall another 10 yen, there would be a powerful incentive for re-establishing carry trades, he said.
Few other currencies are attracting so much interest going into the Denver gathering.
"One of the problems is that everyone is desperate to find forex games to play. People are looking at anything to do with the dollar... Europe is gridlocked at the moment," said Fox.

Wilkes of Bank Julius Baer added: "The Germans don't seem too concerned about the state of the mark, and the U.S. doesn't seem too concerned about the strength of the dollar versus the Europeans. From that point of view, the yen is probably the focus."
